title: AP Biology
summary: Explain molecular mechanisms, inheritance, evolution and ecological change.
frameworkNote: Unit map checked against College Board on 15 October 2026 for the 2026-27 course. Each unit has one focused original revision lesson, not exhaustive topic coverage or an official practice paper. Uses the current eight-unit map and Fall 2025 framework update. These text exercises do not fulfil laboratory requirements.

modules.title: Water polarity and molecular interactions
modules.focus: Connect molecular structure with biological behaviour.
explanation: Water has polar covalent bonds and an uneven distribution of charge. Hydrogen bonds form between molecules, contributing to cohesion and a high specific heat capacity. These interactions are weaker individually than the covalent bonds within a molecule.

Biological macromolecules have properties shaped by their subunits and arrangement. A protein’s amino-acid sequence constrains folding, while side-chain interactions influence its final shape. Changing that shape can alter function without breaking every peptide bond.

workedExample.prompt: Explain why a nonpolar oil droplet separates from water.
steps: Water molecules form favourable interactions with one another, while the oil cannot make comparable polar interactions.
Oil molecules aggregate, reducing the nonpolar surface exposed to water; the mixture separates.

misconception.claim: Heating a protein always changes its amino-acid sequence.
misconception.correction: Denaturation can disrupt folding without hydrolysing the peptide backbone.

questions.prompt: Why can water moderate temperature changes in a habitat?
questions.hint: Connect added heat with intermolecular interactions.
questions.answer: Its high specific heat means substantial energy is needed for a given temperature rise.
checkpoints: Distinguish heat transfer from temperature change.

questions.prompt: A substitution replaces a nonpolar residue inside a protein with a charged residue. Predict a possible consequence.
questions.answer: It may disrupt folding or stability and change function; the effect depends on position and interactions.
checkpoints: Avoid claiming every substitution destroys function.

questions.prompt: A solute has several charged groups. Predict how water molecules orient near a positive group.
questions.answer: Water’s partially negative oxygen ends tend to face the positive group.
checkpoints: Describe orientation rather than claiming a new covalent bond.

questions.hint: Some molecules gain enough energy to escape.
questions.prompt: Why does evaporation cool the remaining water?
questions.answer: Escaping molecules carry energy away, reducing average kinetic energy in the remaining liquid when energy is not fully replaced.
checkpoints: Some molecules gain enough energy to escape.
Escape removes energy from the liquid.
Lower average kinetic energy corresponds to lower temperature.
hints: Some molecules gain enough energy to escape.
Escape removes energy from the liquid.

notes.title: Reasoning through water polarity and molecular interactions
paragraphs: Water’s bent geometry and polar covalent bonds create partial charges that permit hydrogen bonding between molecules. These intermolecular attractions explain cohesion and contribute to high specific heat; they are not the covalent bonds holding each water molecule together. Charged and polar solutes interact favourably with water, whereas nonpolar surfaces tend to aggregate in aqueous environments. Biological macromolecules combine many interactions, so a change in one residue can alter folding without necessarily destroying the entire structure. Connect a molecular property to a specific interaction before predicting a cellular consequence.

workedExamples.prompt: Explain why a drop of water can form a curved surface on a waxy leaf.
steps: Water molecules attract one another through hydrogen bonding, producing cohesion.
The waxy surface is largely nonpolar, giving less favourable adhesion than a strongly polar surface.
Cohesion can therefore maintain a rounded droplet.
workedExamples.conclusion: The shape reflects the balance between water-water cohesion and water-surface adhesion.

flashcards.front: Are hydrogen bonds the O–H covalent bonds inside water?
flashcards.back: No; intermolecular hydrogen bonds are different interactions.

flashcards.front: Why is water polar?
flashcards.back: Polar bonds and bent geometry produce unequal charge distribution.

flashcards.front: What is cohesion?
flashcards.back: Attraction between molecules of the same substance.

flashcards.front: Why do nonpolar surfaces aggregate in water?
flashcards.back: Aggregation reduces their exposed contact with water.

modules.title: Membranes, gradients and surface area
modules.focus: Explain transport without treating membranes as unrestricted barriers.
explanation: A phospholipid bilayer separates compartments and selectively permits passage. Small nonpolar molecules diffuse through it readily, while ions usually require membrane proteins. Passive transport proceeds down an electrochemical gradient without direct energy input from the transport process.

Active transport can move substances against a gradient using an energy source. As a cell grows, its volume increases faster than surface area, reducing exchange area per unit volume. Cells can alter shape or internal organisation to address transport constraints.

workedExample.prompt: Compare surface-area-to-volume ratios of cubes with side lengths 1 and 2 micrometres.
steps: The smaller cube has area 6 and volume 1, giving ratio 6 per micrometre.
The larger has area 24 and volume 8, giving ratio 3 per micrometre, half as large.

misconception.claim: Any transport through a protein is active.
misconception.correction: Facilitated diffusion uses proteins but follows a gradient without direct energy input.

questions.prompt: Two solutions at equal hydrostatic pressure and temperature are separated by a membrane permeable to water but not the dissolved solute. One has a higher concentration of that same solute. Predict net water movement.
questions.hint: Compare solute contributions to water potential with pressure and temperature held equal.
questions.answer: Net water movement is toward the more concentrated solution, which has lower water potential under these conditions.
checkpoints: Describe net rather than one-way molecular motion.

questions.prompt: An ion pump moves ions against their gradient. Why is an energy source required?
questions.hint: The direction is thermodynamically unfavourable by itself.
questions.answer: The pump must couple transport to an energy-releasing process.
checkpoints: Connect coupling to the energy requirement.

questions.prompt: A cube has side 3 µm. Calculate surface-area-to-volume ratio.
questions.answer: 2 µm⁻¹.

questions.prompt: A transporter moves glucose into a cell against its concentration gradient by allowing sodium downhill. Classify the glucose movement.
questions.answer: Secondary active transport.
checkpoints: Sodium movement supplies energy through its gradient.
The coupling makes glucose transport active without direct ATP use by that transporter.
hints: Sodium movement supplies energy through its gradient.

notes.title: Reasoning through membranes, gradients and surface area
paragraphs: A membrane’s selective permeability separates concentration gradients from actual transport rates. Small nonpolar molecules can cross the lipid bilayer readily, while ions usually need transport proteins. Passive transport moves down the relevant electrochemical gradient without direct energy input; active transport couples uphill movement to an energy source. Osmosis depends on water potential, which includes solute and pressure contributions. Cell size matters because surface area grows with length squared while volume grows with length cubed. Larger cells therefore have less exchange surface per unit volume unless shape or internal organisation compensates.

workedExamples.prompt: A cube-shaped cell increases its side from 2 to 4 µm. Compare its surface area and volume changes.
steps: Area scales by the square of the length factor: 2²=4.
Volume scales by its cube: 2³=8.
Thus area per volume is halved.
workedExamples.conclusion: The larger cell has four times the area but eight times the volume.

flashcards.front: What gradient controls passive ion movement?
flashcards.back: The electrochemical gradient, combining concentration and electrical effects.

flashcards.front: Why do ions need membrane proteins?
flashcards.back: Their charge makes crossing the hydrophobic bilayer unfavourable.

flashcards.front: How does doubling a cube’s length change volume?
flashcards.back: It increases eightfold.

flashcards.front: Can pressure affect osmosis?
flashcards.back: Yes; water potential includes pressure as well as solute effects.

modules.title: Enzymes and coupled energy transfer
modules.focus: Distinguish reaction speed from reaction favourability.
explanation: Enzymes lower activation energy and therefore increase reaction rate. They do not change the overall free-energy difference between reactants and products or the equilibrium position. Substrate binding depends on the enzyme’s structure and chemical environment.

Cells couple energy-requiring processes to energy-releasing reactions. Respiration and photosynthesis transfer electrons through organised pathways, using membranes to maintain proton gradients. ATP synthase couples proton movement down a gradient to ATP production.

workedExample.prompt: An enzyme doubles the initial rate in a reaction mixture. Does that show the reaction’s equilibrium has changed?
steps: The observation supports a kinetic effect on how quickly products form.
A catalyst accelerates approach to equilibrium without changing the equilibrium ratio, so the rate result alone does not show a new equilibrium.

misconception.claim: An enzyme makes an unfavourable reaction favourable by lowering activation energy.
misconception.correction: Activation energy concerns the pathway; overall free-energy change determines favourability.

questions.prompt: What happens to ATP production by ATP synthase if a membrane becomes freely permeable to protons?
questions.answer: It decreases because the proton gradient dissipates and less energy is available for coupling.
checkpoints: Connect gradient loss to reduced ATP synthesis.

questions.prompt: Why can very high temperature reduce an enzyme’s rate?
questions.answer: It can disrupt structure and the active site, reducing effective substrate binding or catalysis.
checkpoints: Do not assume all enzymes share one temperature optimum.

questions.prompt: A coupled process has ΔG values +12 and −20 kJ/mol. Find the combined ΔG and its thermodynamic implication.
questions.answer: −8 kJ/mol; the coupled overall process is favourable under the stated conditions.
checkpoints: Interpret the negative result without assuming a fast rate.

questions.hint: Pumping initially continues adding separated protons.
questions.prompt: ATP synthase is inhibited while the respiratory chain initially continues pumping protons. Predict the immediate tendency of the gradient and ATP synthesis.
questions.answer: The gradient tends to build initially, while ATP synthesis through ATP synthase falls.
checkpoints: Pumping initially continues adding separated protons.
The return path through ATP synthase is reduced.
ATP production through that pathway decreases.
hints: Pumping initially continues adding separated protons.
The return path through ATP synthase is reduced.

notes.title: Reasoning through enzymes and coupled energy transfer
paragraphs: Enzymes lower activation energy by providing a favourable reaction pathway, but they do not alter the reaction’s free-energy difference or equilibrium constant. A saturated enzyme population cannot increase its rate indefinitely as substrate concentration rises. Inhibition and temperature changes can affect activity through different mechanisms, so a rate decrease alone does not identify the cause. Cells couple energetically unfavourable processes to favourable ones through shared intermediates or machinery. In chemiosmosis, membrane separation stores electrochemical potential, and proton movement through ATP synthase can drive ATP formation under appropriate conditions.

workedExamples.prompt: An enzyme reaction approaches the same maximum rate with and without a competitive inhibitor, but needs more substrate with the inhibitor. Explain.
steps: A competitive inhibitor competes for the active site.
Increasing substrate concentration can reduce the inhibitor’s relative occupancy.
At high enough substrate, the same limiting catalytic capacity can be approached.
workedExamples.conclusion: The pattern is consistent with competitive inhibition; it does not by itself prove a unique mechanism.

flashcards.front: Does a catalyst change ΔG?
flashcards.back: No; it changes the pathway’s activation barrier.

flashcards.front: What causes saturation?
flashcards.back: Most catalytic sites are occupied, limiting further rate increase.

flashcards.front: What powers ATP synthase?
flashcards.back: A proton electrochemical gradient.

flashcards.front: Why does coupling require a mechanism?
flashcards.back: Favourable and unfavourable processes must be linked to transfer usable energy.

modules.title: Signals and cell-cycle checkpoints
explanation: Cell signalling connects a received signal to a cellular response. A receptor must interact with a compatible ligand or stimulus; downstream relays can amplify the response. Cells with different receptors can respond differently to the same extracellular signal.

Cell-cycle checkpoints regulate progression when conditions or DNA integrity are unsuitable. A mutation that removes checkpoint control can permit division with damage, but one altered pathway does not by itself prove a cell has every property of cancer.

workedExample.prompt: A signal activates a receptor, which activates kinase A, then protein B. Predict the effect of permanently inactive kinase A.
steps: The receptor may still bind the signal, because reception is upstream of A.
If A is required to activate B and no bypass exists, B activation and the downstream response decrease.

misconception.claim: A signal must enter the nucleus directly to change gene expression.
misconception.correction: Membrane receptors can initiate relays that ultimately regulate transcription.

questions.prompt: Why is a no-ligand condition useful in a signalling experiment?
questions.answer: It establishes baseline response for comparison with ligand treatment.
checkpoints: Distinguish background activity from signal-dependent change.

questions.prompt: A damaged cell pauses before DNA replication. What is the value of that checkpoint?
questions.answer: It permits assessment or repair before replication propagates the damage.
checkpoints: Link the pause to genome integrity.

questions.hint: Subtract the baseline in each condition.
questions.prompt: A ligand raises a response from 2 to 10 units. With inhibitor X it rises only from 2 to 3. What comparison supports X reducing ligand-dependent signalling?
questions.answer: The ligand-associated increase falls from 8 to 1 unit with X.
checkpoints: Subtract the baseline in each condition.
The result supports inhibition but does not locate its exact target.
hints: Subtract the baseline in each condition.

questions.hint: Recognise attachment as necessary for accurate segregation.
questions.prompt: Why could failed chromosome attachment trigger a pause before chromosome separation?
questions.answer: A pause allows attachment correction before unequal chromosome segregation occurs.
checkpoints: Recognise attachment as necessary for accurate segregation.
Identify premature separation as the risk.
Connect delay to an opportunity for correction.
hints: Recognise attachment as necessary for accurate segregation.
Identify premature separation as the risk.

notes.title: Reasoning through signals and cell-cycle checkpoints
paragraphs: Cell signalling separates reception, transduction and response. A ligand binds an appropriate receptor, intracellular steps relay or amplify the signal, and target activity changes. The same external signal can produce different responses in cells expressing different receptors or downstream proteins. A pathway diagram represents causal hypotheses; disrupting one component tests only the branches that depend on it. Cell-cycle checkpoints can delay progression when replication or chromosome attachment is incomplete. Loss of checkpoint control increases the chance of propagating errors but does not make every affected cell develop into a tumour.

workedExamples.prompt: A pathway is receptor→A→B→response. A drug blocks the receptor, but an engineered permanently active B restores the response. What does this support?
steps: Receptor blockade normally prevents downstream activation.
Active B bypasses the blocked upstream steps.
Restoration supports B acting downstream of the receptor in this pathway.
workedExamples.conclusion: The result supports the proposed order while leaving alternative bypass mechanisms possible.

flashcards.front: What are the three broad signalling stages?
flashcards.back: Reception, transduction and response.

flashcards.front: What is signal amplification?
flashcards.back: One activated component activates many downstream components.

flashcards.front: Why can one ligand affect cell types differently?
flashcards.back: Their receptors and downstream machinery can differ.

flashcards.front: What is a checkpoint’s role?
flashcards.back: Delay progression until specified conditions are satisfied.

modules.title: Inheritance probabilities and independent events
modules.focus: Use a genetic model with explicit assumptions.
explanation: During meiosis, homologous chromosomes separate and alleles at a locus are distributed to gametes. Independent assortment applies to unlinked genes; genes close together on one chromosome can show linkage instead. Crossing over creates new allele combinations.

Punnett squares describe probabilities, not a guaranteed count in a small family. Dominance describes a heterozygote’s phenotype under a model, not an allele’s frequency or biological superiority. State assumptions about dominance and linkage before multiplying probabilities.

workedExample.prompt: For Aa×Aa under complete dominance, find the probability of the recessive phenotype.
steps: Each parent contributes a with probability 1/2.
The aa genotype has probability (1/2)(1/2)=1/4 and shows the recessive phenotype.

misconception.claim: A dominant allele must be the most common allele.
misconception.correction: Dominance concerns phenotype in a heterozygote; frequency is a population property.

questions.prompt: For AaBb×aabb with unlinked loci, find P(aabb).
checkpoints: P(bb)=1/2 and the loci assort independently.

questions.prompt: Why might linked genes depart from a predicted independent-assortment ratio?
questions.answer: Nearby alleles tend to travel together unless crossing over separates them.

questions.hint: The Aa parent produces A and a with equal probability.
questions.prompt: For Aa×aa under complete dominance, find the genotype ratio and dominant-phenotype probability.
questions.answer: Aa:aa=1:1; dominant phenotype probability 1/2.
checkpoints: The Aa parent produces A and a with equal probability.
The aa parent contributes only a.
Half the offspring are Aa and half aa.
hints: The Aa parent produces A and a with equal probability.
The aa parent contributes only a.

questions.prompt: For unlinked AaBb×AaBb, find P(aa and dominant B phenotype).

notes.title: Reasoning through inheritance probabilities and independent events
paragraphs: Inheritance probabilities rely on explicit assumptions about alleles, segregation, dominance and linkage. A Punnett square lists possible gamete combinations rather than guaranteeing the composition of every small family. For independent events, multiply probabilities; for mutually exclusive ways to reach an outcome, add them. Dominance concerns phenotype expression in a heterozygote and does not make an allele more frequent or beneficial. Linked loci may produce non-independent gametes, with recombination modifying their frequencies. Sex-linked problems additionally require tracking the chromosome carrying each allele and the relevant parental transmission.

workedExamples.prompt: For Aa×Aa, find the probability that exactly one of two offspring is aa, assuming independent births.
steps: Each offspring has P(aa)=1/4 and P(not aa)=3/4.
There are two mutually exclusive orders: aa then not aa, or the reverse.

flashcards.front: When are probabilities multiplied?
flashcards.back: For a sequence of independent events, or using appropriate conditional probabilities.

flashcards.front: When are probabilities added?
flashcards.back: For mutually exclusive ways to obtain the outcome.

flashcards.front: Does dominant mean common?
flashcards.back: No.

flashcards.front: Why can linked loci violate independent assortment predictions?
flashcards.back: Their alleles can be transmitted together more often than independent gamete models predict.

modules.title: From a DNA sequence to a regulated protein
modules.focus: Keep transcription and translation directions explicit.
explanation: Transcription builds RNA using a DNA template, and translation reads mRNA codons to assemble a polypeptide. RNA is synthesised in the 5′ to 3′ direction. A coding DNA strand matches the RNA sequence except that RNA uses U in place of T.

Regulation controls when, where and how much gene product is made. A mutation may alter coding sequence, RNA processing or regulation. A synonymous change preserves the encoded amino acid at that codon, but other changes can shift the reading frame or create a stop.

workedExample.prompt: A coding DNA segment is 5′-ATG GAA-3′. Write the corresponding mRNA sequence.
steps: Keep the coding-strand order and direction because it already matches the RNA orientation.
Replace T with U: 5′-AUG GAA-3′.

misconception.claim: Every mutation changes the amino-acid sequence.
misconception.correction: Some are synonymous or outside the translated region, although they can still have other effects.

questions.prompt: A single nucleotide is inserted near the start of a coding sequence. What can happen to the reading frame?
questions.hint: Codons are read in groups of three.
questions.answer: A frameshift can change downstream codons and possibly introduce an early stop.
checkpoints: The insertion is not a multiple of three.

questions.prompt: Why can two cell types contain the same DNA but produce different proteins?
questions.answer: They express different subsets of genes or express them at different levels.

questions.hint: Use the coding rather than template convention.
questions.prompt: A coding strand is 5′-GCT TTT-3′. Write its mRNA counterpart.
questions.answer: 5′-GCU UUU-3′.
checkpoints: Use the coding rather than template convention.
hints: Use the coding rather than template convention.

questions.hint: Codons are read in groups of three.
questions.prompt: Compare deletion of one coding nucleotide with deletion of three adjacent coding nucleotides.
questions.answer: One usually shifts the downstream frame; three preserve the downstream frame while altering or removing amino-acid information.
checkpoints: Codons are read in groups of three.
A one-base change disrupts that grouping downstream.
Three bases leave the later frame intact, though the protein can still be affected.
hints: Codons are read in groups of three.
A one-base change disrupts that grouping downstream.

notes.title: Reasoning through from a DNA sequence to a regulated protein
paragraphs: Transcription copies information from a DNA template into RNA using complementary base pairing and antiparallel orientation. The coding strand matches the RNA sequence except for T versus U, but it is not the strand read as the template. Translation reads mRNA codons in a specified frame and joins amino acids according to the genetic code. A substitution may be silent, missense or nonsense depending on its position and resulting codon. Insertions or deletions not divisible by three can shift the downstream frame. Gene regulation changes when and how much a product is made without necessarily changing DNA sequence.

workedExamples.prompt: Transcribe template DNA 3′-TAC CTT-5′ and identify the first mRNA codon.
steps: Pair T with A, A with U, C with G and T with A.
Write the RNA antiparallel as 5′-AUG GAA-3′.
The first codon is AUG.
workedExamples.conclusion: The mRNA is 5′-AUG GAA-3′; AUG is a start codon in the usual translation context.

flashcards.front: Which strand matches mRNA apart from T/U?
flashcards.back: The coding DNA strand, written in the same direction.

flashcards.front: Which direction is RNA synthesised?
What insertion can cause a frameshift?
flashcards.back: A coding insertion whose length is not divisible by three.

flashcards.front: Can expression differ with identical DNA?
flashcards.back: Yes, through regulatory and cellular differences.

modules.title: Allele frequencies and selection
modules.focus: Separate population change from individual need.
explanation: Natural selection changes population composition when heritable variation affects reproductive success in an environment. Individuals do not acquire a needed allele because selection demands it. Mutation, migration and genetic drift can also change allele frequencies.

Hardy-Weinberg proportions provide a null model under specific assumptions, including random mating and absence of selection, migration, mutation and strong drift. With two alleles, p+q=1 and expected genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q².

workedExample.prompt: A population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium has recessive genotype frequency 0.09. Find the expected heterozygote frequency.
steps: The expected heterozygote frequency is 2pq=2(0.7)(0.3)=0.42.

misconception.claim: Individuals evolve new adaptations because they need them.
misconception.correction: Selection changes frequencies of heritable variants across generations.

questions.prompt: If p=0.8 and q=0.2 under equilibrium, find the expected homozygous recessive frequency.
checkpoints: Do not confuse q with q².

questions.prompt: A storm randomly kills most individuals in a small population. Which mechanism can shift allele frequencies?
questions.hint: Survival is random with respect to the allele.
questions.answer: Genetic drift through a population bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium q=0.4. Find p² and 2pq.

questions.hint: Small populations experience sampling variation in transmission.
questions.prompt: Two alleles are initially equally frequent in several small isolated populations. Their frequencies diverge without consistent environmental differences. What mechanism is consistent with this pattern?
questions.answer: Genetic drift is consistent with random divergence across small populations.
checkpoints: Small populations experience sampling variation in transmission.
The pattern supports a drift explanation without proving selection absent.
hints: Small populations experience sampling variation in transmission.

notes.title: Reasoning through allele frequencies and selection
paragraphs: Allele frequency counts gene copies, whereas genotype frequency counts individuals. In a diploid population each individual contributes two copies at an autosomal locus. Hardy-Weinberg proportions are a null-model prediction under specified conditions, not a statement that real populations never evolve. Selection requires heritable variation associated with reproductive success; individuals do not acquire useful alleles because they need them. Drift can shift frequencies by chance, especially in small populations. A phenotype-frequency change alone may reflect environment, so genetic evidence is needed before concluding that allele frequencies changed.

workedExamples.prompt: A population contains 20 AA, 30 Aa and 50 aa individuals. Find p, the A frequency.
steps: There are 200 allele copies among 100 diploid individuals.
A copies total 2(20)+30=70.
Divide 70 by 200.
workedExamples.conclusion: p=0.35 and q=0.65; these counts need not satisfy equilibrium proportions.

flashcards.front: How many autosomal allele copies does a diploid individual contribute?
flashcards.back: Two.

flashcards.front: What is heterozygote frequency under Hardy-Weinberg assumptions?
flashcards.back: 2pq.

flashcards.front: Does selection create alleles because they are needed?
flashcards.back: No.

flashcards.front: Where is random drift often strongest?
flashcards.back: In small populations.

modules.title: Population growth and ecosystem energy
modules.focus: Track both rate limits and energy transfers.
explanation: Population growth depends on births, deaths, immigration and emigration. Logistic models reduce growth as population size approaches a carrying-capacity parameter, reflecting density-dependent constraints. Real carrying capacity can change with resources and conditions.

Energy enters many ecosystems through primary production and leaves as dissipated heat; matter cycles through organisms and surroundings. Transfer efficiency between trophic levels varies, so a stated efficiency is a model parameter rather than an exact universal constant.

workedExample.prompt: An ecosystem’s producers store 20,000 kJ. Under an assumed 10% transfer at each level, how much reaches secondary consumers?
steps: Primary consumers receive 0.1(20,000)=2,000 kJ.
Secondary consumers receive 0.1(2,000)=200 kJ.

misconception.claim: Energy cycles indefinitely through an ecosystem like nutrients.
misconception.correction: Energy flows and dissipates as heat; nutrients are recycled.

questions.prompt: A population gains 50 births and 12 immigrants, with 30 deaths and 8 emigrants. Find net change.
questions.answer: +24 individuals.

questions.prompt: In logistic growth, what is the predicted net growth at N=K?
questions.answer: Zero in the model.
checkpoints: This does not imply all births and deaths stop.

questions.prompt: Producers store 8,000 kJ; herbivores receive 12% and carnivores receive 20% of herbivore energy. Find carnivore energy.
For dN/dt=0.2N(1−N/500), find growth at N=250 and N=500.
questions.answer: 25 individuals per time unit and 0 respectively.
checkpoints: At capacity the limiting factor is zero.

notes.title: Reasoning through population growth and ecosystem energy
paragraphs: Population size changes through births, deaths, immigration and emigration, while population growth rate also depends on the time interval. Exponential growth assumes a constant per-capita rate; logistic growth introduces a density-dependent limiting factor. Carrying capacity is a model parameter that can change with resources and conditions rather than a permanent species property. Ecosystem energy flows through trophic transfers and ultimately dissipates as heat, whereas matter cycles through organisms and physical reservoirs. Transfer efficiency is a measured or assumed fraction for a particular transfer, not a universal law fixing every ecosystem at ten per cent.

workedExamples.prompt: A population of 200 has 30 births, 20 deaths, 8 immigrants and 3 emigrants in one year. Find final size and percentage net change.
steps: Net change is 30−20+8−3=15.
Final size is 215.
Relative change is 15/200=0.075.
workedExamples.conclusion: The population increases by 7.5% over that year.

flashcards.front: What four flows change population size?
flashcards.back: Births, deaths, immigration and emigration.

flashcards.front: What is the logistic limiting factor?
Does energy cycle like matter?
flashcards.back: No; energy flows and dissipates, while matter cycles.

flashcards.front: Is trophic transfer always 10%?
flashcards.back: No; efficiency varies and must be measured or stated.
